newsitem.title: UK: New bid launched to ban cosmetics tests on animals.
newsitem.headline: New bid launched to ban cosmetics tests on animals.

text.p: Animal welfare groups and retailers joined forces on Tuesday to launch their own international standard to guarantee against testing cosmetics on animals.
Disappointed by the failure of the European Union to institute a planned ban by the beginning of next year, they said they would try to encourage manufacturers and retailers to do it on their own.

"Many people genuinely believe cosmetics and toiletries are no longer tested on animals," Mike Baker, chief executive of the British Union for the Abolition of Vivisection (BUAV), told a news conference.
But, he said, more than 30,000 animals were still killed every year in cosmetics testing in Europe. "Animals are poisoned, they are blinded, or they are forced to endure irritating substances."

The European Commission had planned a ban on cosmetics testing on animals starting on January 1, 1998, but abandoned this deadline when it became clear that what it considered acceptable alternatives would not be available by then.
The alternative is clear to Baker, who said surveys had shown more than 80 percent of European consumers disapproved of testing cosmetics on animals.
"Use the more than 8,000 ingredients that are already on the market and shown to be safe," he said. "We do not need another 'magic ingredient' in mascara (or) a wrinkle cream."

The BUAV, European Coalition to End Animal Experiments, the U.S. Humane Society and other groups are backing the initiative, as are British companies like supermarket chains Tesco and Sainsbury, the Body Shop and Paul Mitchell, a maker of hair-care products.
Baker said 99 companies had signed up so far, agreeing not to sell anything that had been tested on animals or that contained ingredients that had been.
"We believe we will genuinely become a world-wide initiative," said Roger Gale, a member of Britain's parliament and chairman of its animal welfare committee.
"We feel let down by the Council of Ministers, by the European Commission, by the European Union," he added.
"What we have is an almost unbeatable combination of public opinion...and commercial clout," Gale said.
"Companies that animal-test can ignore groups like us. They can't ignore customers," Baker agreed.

The European Cosmetic, Toiletry and Perfumery Association (COLIPA) defends the delay in an animal testing ban, saying alternative methods, such as computer modelling and using human skin tissue in test tubes, have not been evaluated.
Animal welfare groups say testing is not only cruel but unscientific, as animals often react very differently from humans to drugs and chemicals.
